title: The Statement
full_review:
A Nazi collaborator tries to outrun his past in the tautly paced but ideologically skewed chess-game thriller "The Statement" (Sony Classics).

Directed by Norman Jewison, the film explores controversial accusations surrounding the Catholic Church's alleged protection of war criminals in the years and decades following World War II. However, while the story is loosely based on factual events, Jewison jettisons objectivity in favor of broad-brushstroke anticlericalism, painting the Catholic hierarchy for the most part as a den of duplicitous vipers willing to cover up atrocities for the greater good (read "public image") of the church.

Michael Caine stars as Pierre Brossard, a fictitious character based on real-life Paul Touvier, a Frenchman who was convicted in 1994 for war crimes committed during the Second World War. As a young man, Brossard, a Catholic, had been an intelligence officer for the Vichy government -- the French puppet regime which collaborated with the German occupiers -- and had ordered the execution of seven Jews. The heinous act, depicted in the opening sequence, is made more unsettling by Jewison's electing to photograph it in grainy black-and-white -- an artistic decision which, while separating it aesthetically from the rest of the film, gives it a heightened cinema-verite immediacy.

The story then jumps ahead to 1992, where Brossard, now in his 70s, is living an anonymous and seemingly repentant life in southern France -- his Provencal peace secured by a presidential pardon and the benediction of "right-wing" power-players in the Catholic Church who shelter him in a rotating shuffle of sympathetic monasteries.

When a hit man -- hired by an apparent "Jewish" vigilante group seeking redress for Brossard's past sins -- attempts to assassinate the sinister senior on a deserted stretch of road, Brossard turns the table on his would-be-killer and beats him to the draw. Realizing he has been marked for death, Brossard seeks safe passage out of the country. While awaiting his passport Brossard is protected by a shadowy network of high-ranking politicos and prelates bound by loyalty to a mysterious fraternity known as the Chevaliers -- just one of the narrative threads left dangling by the, at times, murky plot.

Complicating his escape is a bulldog Parisian judge (Tilda Swinton), who, despite the aforementioned clemency, reopens the investigation into Brossard's wartime activities by invoking newly passed "crimes against humanity" legislation. Relentless in her pursuit to bring Brossard to justice, she enlists the help of a scrupulous gendarme, Col. Roux (Jeremy Northam), setting in motion the ensuing cat-and-mouse game forcing Brossard to stay one step ahead of the law and two steps ahead of the assassins' cross hairs.

Part of the problem with "The Statement" is that Jewison never seems to decide whether he wants to make a serious study of the abuse of power or a John le Carre cloak-and-dagger thriller. And while the film is bracketed with text that gives the tale an air of weightiness, much of what happens in between is more fiction than fact, regrettably using a sensitive subject matter as fodder for commercial melodrama.

Like Laurence Olivier in "Marathon Man," Caine's Brossard is at once both menacing and deceptively fragile. He brings an eerie combination of cold-hearted calculation and contrition to the role -- though his near-psychotic, self-flagellating Catholic guilt borders on caricature.

Yet, while the character of Brossard flirts with parody, the clergy depicted in the film are walking stereotypes. The Catholic hierarchy is portrayed as a bunch of equivocating navel-gazers who, if not implicated in war crime cover-ups directly, adhere to a rigid circle-the-wagons reactionary mentality that protects "devout" monsters like Brossard by placing more concern with the self-interest of the church than exposing the injustices perpetrated by its members.

And though Jewison does make sure to sidestep the card of "anti-Catholicism" by including a "nice" Jesuit priest, such blink-and-you'll-miss-it nods to piety are but a drop in the bucket of hypocrisy and ecclesiastical indifference presented by the film -- one character goes so far as to say that the corruption "goes all the way up to Rome."

Brossard is a daily communicant, devoted to the Blessed Mother and St. Christopher. He is also a cold-blooded killer who doesn't like kneeling next to blacks in church and accuses post-Tridentine "leftist" priests of ruining the Catholic faith -- not to mention that he loves kicking dogs. One priest is an anti-Semite. Another, the French cardinal involved in the case, has on his mantle a framed portrait of Pope Pius XII -- the WWII-era pontiff whom some have criticized for not speaking out against Hitler's persecution of the Jews. Conversely, the film's heroes are a lapsed Catholic and an agnostic.

In the future, it would be nice if filmmakers refrained from making such blanket "statements."

Due to sporadic violence and anti-clerical characterizations, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
